---
title: "Methods"
---


### Study Population

The Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility-Reykjavik Study (AGES-Reykjavik) is a population-based cohort study initiated in 2002 as a continuation of the Reykjavik Study, which had followed residents of Reykjavik, Iceland since 1967 [@RN1]. The AGES-Reykjavik cohort was drawn from surviving members of the original Reykjavik Study cohort (born 1907-1935). Study protocols were approved by the National Bioethics Committee in Iceland (VSN-00-063), the National Institute on Aging Intramural Institutional Review Board, and the Icelandic Data Protection Authority. All participants provided written informed consent.

The present analysis included 2,491 participants with available DNA methylation data and dementia diagnoses, comprising 1,065 males (42.8%) and 1,426 females (57.2%). At baseline, the median age was 75.0 years (interquartile range: 72.0-80.0 years). Smoking status was classified as never (n=1,088, 43.7%), former (n=1,118, 44.9%), or current smoker (n=285, 11.4%) (@supptbl-covariate). Participants were followed for up to 13.4 years through 2015, with cognitive assessments conducted at baseline (2002-2006) and during follow-up examinations.

### Dementia Assessment and Classification

Assessment and follow-up of cognitive status was based on 2,491 subjects with methylation data and ascertained cognitive status over a mean and maximal follow-up time of 8.8 and 13.4 years. Dementia diagnoses followed a three-step process including initial cognitive screening of the total baseline sample, detailed neuropsychological testing for step 1 screen-positives, and among those who screened positive in step 2, a comprehensive neurologic examination and a proxy interview. Final diagnoses, based on the totality of data collected by questionnaire, depression, physical and sensory function, and laboratory data were adjudicated by a consensus panel (geriatrician, neurologist, neuroradiologist, and neuropsychologist) and diagnosed following international criteria. MCI was defined at AGES study visits at baseline and approximately 5 years later. Incident dementia cases and normal status were identified through follow-up examinations, nursing home assessments, medical records, and death certificates through 2015 [@RN1; @RN63].
 
Based on cognitive status at baseline and follow-up, participants were categorized into six groups (@tbl-dementia-category). Of the 2,174 participants who were cognitively normal at baseline, 1,581 (72.7%) maintained normal cognition throughout follow-up (stable normal), 99 (4.6%) progressed to mild cognitive impairment (normal2mci), and 494 (22.7%) developed incident dementia (normal2incid). Among 156 participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline, 49 (31.4%) remained cognitively stable (stable_mci), and 107 (68.6%) progressed to dementia (mci2incid). The normal2mci and stable_mci groups could include participants who might experience cognitive improvement to normal status at follow-up. The remaining 161 participants (6.5%) had prevalent dementia at study entry. Notably, no participants in the normal2mci or stable_mci groups progressed to dementia during the 13.4-year follow-up period.

### Processing of DNA Methylation Data

Whole blood-derived DNA samples were processed, bisulfite-converted, and assayed at the Huge-F facility at Erasmus Medical Center (Rotterdam, the Netherlands) using Illumina's Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip V1 Manifest B5 platform (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA), which interrogates over 850,000 CpG sites across the genome. Bisulfite conversion was performed using the Zymo EZ-96 DNA Methylation Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA).

Quality control was also conducted by the Huge-F facility at both sample and probe levels as described in [@RN64; @RN65; @RN66]. At the sample level, 18 samples were flagged based on control metrics shown in the Illumina BeadArray Controls Reporter Software, and 5 samples were excluded for low call rate (detection p > 0.01 in ≥4% of probes). At the probe level, 1,851 probes with detection p ≥ 0.01 in ≥10% of samples were removed, along with 1,258 probes with bead count < 3. Additionally, 43,254 cross-reactive probes, as well as probes overlapping with single nucleotide polymorphisms, EPIC v1-specific problematic probes, and sex chromosome probes were excluded. Raw intensity data underwent quantile normalization. After quality control procedures, 799,149 CpG sites were retained for subsequent analyses. M-values were used for all statistical analyses due to their superior statistical properties for differential methylation analysis compared to beta values.


### Dementia Association Analysis

We performed an epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) testing differential DNA methylation across dementia trajectory groups. For each of the 799,149 CpG sites, methylation M-values were regressed on dementia status, adjusting for age, sex, smoking status, and six white blood cell type proportions: M-value~i~ = β~0~ + β~1~·dementia_status + β~2~·age + β~3~·sex + β~4~·smoking + β~5–10~·WBC_proportions + ε~i~. Adding plate number to the model produced highly similar associations, likely because the M-values were quantile-normalized across all samples. 

Dementia status was coded as a six-level categorical variable with stable normal cognition as the reference group, yielding five contrasts (stable_mci, normal2mci, normal2incid, mci2incid, and prevalent dementia). Sex was coded with male as the reference category and smoking status with non-smoker as the reference category. White blood cell proportions (B lymphocytes, CD4+ T lymphocytes, CD8+ T lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils) were estimated from DNA methylation data [@RN67] (Supplementary Table [-@supptbl-covariate], [-@supptbl-exemplar]).

Genome-wide significance was defined at *P* < 1.0 × 10⁻⁸, which is slightly more stringent than the Bonferroni correction for the number of CpG sites tested (0.05 / 799,149 = 6.26 × 10⁻⁸). Results are also presented at less stringent thresholds for sensitivity analyses. Analyses were conducted in R (v4.5.2) using `stats::lm()` for linear regression, with parallel processing via the furrr and future packages. Model results were extracted with `broom::tidy()`.

Ordinary linear regression was used rather than Cox proportional hazards models. The dementia trajectory classification involves multiple starting states (cognitively normal, MCI, prevalent dementia) and multiple endpoints, a multi-state structure that does not conform to the single-origin, time-to-event framework of survival models. Linear regression also provided a unified covariate-adjustment framework across the EWAS, the methylation-residual computation that feeds UMAP and VAE, and the downstream analyses. Key associations replicated across independent cohorts (ADNI/AIBL and AddNeuroMed; @fig-validation).

### Gene Annotation

We performed comprehensive gene annotation for CpG sites using both the Illumina (UCSC) gene annotation and the Genomic Regions Enrichment of Annotations Tool (GREAT) [@RN68]. For the GREAT analysis, we created a BED file containing genomic coordinates of all CpG sites from the Illumina MethylationEPIC BeadChip. Using the default "basal plus extension" approach, GREAT assigns each gene a regulatory domain that extends 5 kb upstream and 1 kb downstream from its transcription start site. This domain is then extended up to 1 Mb in both directions until reaching the regulatory domains of neighboring genes. Each CpG site is subsequently associated with all genes whose regulatory domains it overlaps, enabling a systematic mapping of potential regulatory relationships.


### Gene Ontology Enrichment Analysis

We performed Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis for biological processes using the enrichGO function from the clusterProfiler R package (version 4.16.0) [@RN69]. For each dementia transition, CpG sites were ranked by their association p-values from the genome-wide analysis, and the top 1,000 and 2,000 CpG sites were selected. Their corresponding GREAT-annotated genes were mapped to Entrez gene identifiers using the org.Hs.eg.db annotation database and used as input for enrichment analysis. This rank-based selection was adopted because applying a common genome-wide significance threshold produced highly unequal numbers of CpG sites across transitions, leaving some transition groups with too few genes for meaningful enrichment analysis. By selecting a fixed number of top-ranked CpG sites, comparable gene set sizes were obtained for each transition, enabling balanced comparison of enriched biological processes. The background gene set comprised all GREAT-annotated genes associated with CpG sites on the Illumina MethylationEPIC BeadChip. Enrichment was performed separately for each dementia transition and CpG threshold, using Gene Ontology biological process terms with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing. Enrichment was considered statistically significant at an adjusted p-value < 0.05.

To identify biological processes unique to individual disease stages, we determined transition-specific GO terms, defined as terms significantly enriched in exactly one dementia transition. Transition-specific GO terms were then grouped into functional categories to facilitate biological interpretation (Supplementary Table [-@supptbl-top1000-normal2mci]–[-@supptbl-top1000-prev], Supplementary Data [-@suppdata-GO_top1000]–[-@suppdata-GO_top2000]). Commonly used redundancy reduction tools such as REVIGO and the simplify function in clusterProfiler compute pairwise semantic similarity among enriched terms and retain only the most significant representative from each cluster, effectively discarding the remaining terms. Because this study aimed to comprehensively characterize the biological processes engaged at each disease stage rather than to produce a minimal list of non-redundant terms, we instead retained all significantly enriched terms and classified them into predefined functional categories. We developed a keyword-based categorization function that assigns each GO term to one of 22 biological function categories — including Synaptic Function and Organization, Neural Development and Regulation, Immune Response, Ion Transport and Regulation, Extracellular Matrix Organization, Vascular Development, and Cellular Signaling — through priority-ordered pattern matching against GO term descriptions. Categories were arranged from specific patterns (e.g., "synaptic vesicle" for Synaptic Vesicle Control) to broader patterns (e.g., "develop" or "differentiat" for Development and Differentiation) to minimize misclassification, and selected categories incorporated exclusion rules to improve specificity. Terms not matching any category remained unassigned. For example, terms related to extracellular matrix organization (GO:0030198), extracellular structure organization (GO:0043062), and positive regulation of collagen biosynthetic process (GO:0032967) were categorized under "Extracellular Matrix Organization" (@supptbl-top1000-normal2mci). Similarly, terms involving regulation of postsynapse organization (GO:0099175), modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential (GO:0098815), and postsynapse assembly (GO:0099068) were grouped under "Synaptic Function and Organization" (@supptbl-top1000-normal2mci).

### UMAP Dimensionality Reduction

We applied Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) to analyze DNA methylation patterns at two significance thresholds: 403 DMPs at P < 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ and 949 DMPs at P < 1.0 × 10⁻⁷. Prior to dimensionality reduction, methylation values were adjusted for potential confounding factors via linear regression using the same set of covariates as EWAS analysis except dementia transitions. The regression residuals were centered and scaled, then used as input for UMAP analysis, implemented through the uwot package (version 0.2.4) with the following hyperparameters: n_neighbors = 10, min_dist = 0.5, n_components = 6, and Euclidean distance metric.

To reduce sensitivity to random initialization, UMAP was run five times with different random seeds (123, 223, 323, 423, 523) and the resulting embeddings were averaged element-wise to produce a single stable representation per subject. To assess sensitivity to hyperparameter choices, a grid of 25 parameter combinations was evaluated by crossing five n_neighbors values (10, 15, 20, 30, 50) with five min_dist values (0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8). Trajectory separation was quantified using a density-based dementia progression score, and the selected combination (n_neighbors = 10, min_dist = 0.5) produced the clearest trajectory separation across dementia categories, though qualitatively similar patterns were observed across other parameter combinations.

### VAE Dimensionality Reduction

We also employed a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), a deep learning method based on neural networks, to learn a probabilistic latent representation of DNA methylation patterns. While UMAP preserves local neighborhood structure through graph-based optimization, the VAE learns a generative model that captures nonlinear relationships through encoder-decoder neural networks, providing a complementary perspective on the underlying data structure.

The VAE architecture consisted of a symmetric encoder-decoder with four hidden layers (512, 256, 128, and 64 units) using ReLU activations, batch normalization, and dropout regularization (0.05–0.1). The encoder mapped input methylation values to a 6-dimensional latent space via the reparameterization trick, and the decoder reconstructed the original input from the latent representation (@suppfig-vae-methodology). The model was trained using the Adam optimizer (learning rate = 0.001) with a composite loss function combining mean squared error for reconstruction and KL divergence for regularization, weighted by a beta parameter. Training was extended to 150 epochs with an early stopping patience of 40 epochs to allow discovery of subtle biological signals, supplemented by learning rate reduction on plateau (factor = 0.5, patience = 20 epochs).

To systematically select the beta parameter, we evaluated eight values (0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0006, 0.001, 0.002, 0.003, 0.005, 0.01) across both significance thresholds. Several beta values produced qualitatively similar methylation patterns, and beta = 0.001 was selected for subsequent analyses. To guard against overfitting, the VAE was trained using 5-fold stratified cross-validation, with folds stratified by dementia transition category. The latent representations from all five folds were averaged to produce a single stable embedding per subject. The VAE was implemented using Keras 3 (keras3 v1.5.1) with the TensorFlow backend (v2.20.0) in R.

### Dementia Progression Score

Both UMAP and VAE produced 6-component embeddings, yielding 15 pairwise 2D projections. To quantify how well each 2D projection captured a smooth, directional trajectory through the six dementia categories, we developed a dementia progression score (DPS). DPS is the product of two components: path efficiency, which measures how straight the centroid path is, and mean directional cosine, which measures whether the path proceeds in the expected progression direction. The score ranges from $-1$ to $+1$, where values near $+1$ indicate centroids forming a straight-line path in the expected progression order, values near $0$ indicate no detectable progression signal, and values near $-1$ indicate reversed ordering.

For each dementia category in a given 2D projection, a density peak was identified using two-dimensional kernel density estimation (KDE) via `MASS::kde2d`. Grid points exceeding the 90th percentile of the estimated density surface were retained, and their mean coordinates served as the centroid for that category. The six centroids were then ordered by expected dementia progression severity: normal2mci, stable_normal, stable_mci, normal2incid, mci2incid, and prev_dementia.

Given $n = 6$ ordered centroids $(x_i, y_i)$, step vectors and Euclidean distances between consecutive centroids were computed as:

$$\Delta x_i = x_{i+1} - x_i, \quad \Delta y_i = y_{i+1} - y_i, \quad d_i = \sqrt{\Delta x_i^2 + \Delta y_i^2}$$

The total path length and direct end-to-end distance, i.e., from the first transition normal2mci to the last prev_dementia, were defined as:

$$L_{\text{path}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} d_i, \qquad L_{\text{direct}} = \sqrt{(x_n - x_1)^2 + (y_n - y_1)^2}$$

Path efficiency, bounded in $[0, 1]$ by the triangle inequality, was computed as the ratio $E = L_{\text{direct}} / L_{\text{path}}$. A unit vector of progression direction was defined from the normal2mci centroid to the prev_dementia centroid:

$$\hat{\mathbf{p}} = \frac{1}{L_{\text{direct}}} \begin{pmatrix} x_n - x_1 \\ y_n - y_1 \end{pmatrix}$$

For each step, the cosine of the angle between the step vector and the progression direction was computed as:

$$\cos \theta_i = \frac{\Delta x_i \cdot \hat{p}_x + \Delta y_i \cdot \hat{p}_y}{d_i}$$

The mean directional cosine $C = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \cos \theta_i$ lies in $[-1, 1]$, where $+1$ indicates perfect forward alignment and $-1$ indicates complete reversal. The final score was computed as:

$$\text{DPS} = E \times C = \frac{L_{\text{direct}}}{L_{\text{path}}} \times \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \cos \theta_i$$

To evaluate the statistical significance of the observed DPS in each 2D latent plane, we performed a label permutation test with 1,000 iterations. In each permutation, the dementia category labels were randomly shuffled across subjects while the embedding coordinates remained fixed, and DPS was recomputed for all 15 dimension pairs. This produced a null distribution under the hypothesis of no association between dementia group membership and methylation-derived embedding positions. Empirical p-values were computed as the proportion of permutations yielding a DPS greater than or equal to the observed value. DPS and the permutation test were applied identically to both UMAP and VAE embeddings, and dimension pairs were ranked by DPS. A path must be simultaneously efficient and correctly oriented to score near $+1$.

### Data analysis and statistical methods

Data analyses were primarily conducted using the tidyverse suite of packages in R version 4.5.2. Various statistical tests, including correlation test, t-test, ANOVA, and chi-square test, were conducted using the R package `rstatix` (version 0.7.3) since it provides a pipe-friendly framework coherent with the `tidyverse` suite. Data visualization was implemented using ggplot2 (version 4.0.2) and its extensions (ggtext (version 0.1.2), ComplexUpset (version 1.3.3), geomtextpath (version 0.2.0)), with multi-panel figures assembled using the patchwork package (version 1.3.2). Tables were made using the `gt` package (version 1.3.0).
